Author: @2Ania
Content:
This is a very interesting topic and video overall. But there are quite a few issues with the script. One thing is just plain wrong: China has natural gas coming from Russia via the Power of Siberia pipeline. 
The video also talks about a coming reduction in gas/LNG that counters the facts: In the U.S. alone, there are LNG terminals already being built or expanded, and the current administration is an avid supporter of LNG. Russia plans to expand its pipeline network in Asia. China is the largest client at the moment with plans for a Power of Siberia 2 pipeline linking it to Russia via a different route. Plus the U.S. seems set to ease sanctions, then Russia will be able to (openly) export more gas to Asia to satisfy the growing demand. 
South Korea and Japan currently do not have natural gas pipelines linking them to other countries, but both countries are exploring options to increase their sources of energy which involve gas. One plan is to interconnect energy grids between various Asian countries including South Korea; The plan would include gas power plants. Another option being considered is a gas interconnection plan between ASEAN countries that may include Japan. Indonesia and Malaysia are ASEAN countries that have offshore gas fields. There are geopolitical and financial hurdles, but pipelines already exist between some ASEAN countries. Whether piped or via LNG transport, importing gas between ASEAN countries is highly desirable because the shorter distance between producers and consumers would lower the price of gas, and doing so would diversify energy sources for gas intensive and emerging economies in the region.
Lastly, at ~12:40 the transcript says that most of the big suppliers are far away and across oceans that make any sort of pipeline project infeasible. Perhaps this is meant to refer to China (which is increasing piped gas from Russia), South Korea and Japan; but it seems to imply that pipelines cannot be built across long distances with large bodies of water.
 This is untrue: Natural gas is piped from offshore rigs to the mainland just like oil. Also, natural gas from Russia had been going all the way to Germany and beyond, passing under the Baltic Sea (via NordStream 1, plus NordStream 2 before it was destroyed by... someone). There are also pipelines across the Mediterranean Between Algeria and Italy, etc.
Other comments have made these and other points. I think it would be worthwhile to consider these suggestions and re-cut the video or at least add notes to it, given how important the topic is and how many people will watch it as their main and only source of information about it.

Content: I don't know if your prediction that gas might become less relevant at the end is true. It might become true if gas becomes much more scarce and therefore expensive, but otherwise it doesn't seem like it's going anywhere. If you have a central gas hookup in your apartment, most of what you're paying for is probably the infrastructure, not the actual gas. It's also cheap enough to generate general electricity, and considered clean enough that it's not harmful to people's health even if they live across the street from a power plant (at least in developed countries with strict regulations). Sure there are some niche uses that could become less common, e.g. CNG vehicles, but it's a small fraction of the total global gas consumption.

Author: @mceajc
Content:
I had the distinct pleasure of visiting the Spadeadam site in the UK (where rockets used to be developed), but was repurposed to safety testing gas pipelines (amongst other hazardous testing). In order to test that pipelines are "safe", they have to show that, should a crack develop and propagate, the depressurisation front of the internal gas (its local speed of sound) travels faster than the speed of the crack propagation.

So, for example, a 20-inch pipe is buried to standard depth, and cooled to -20 degrees Celsius (steel is more brittle and fracture-prone the colder it is).

Then they set off an explosive charge. On a pipe filled with pressurised natural gas. The explosions were regularly heard many miles away.

The pipe has been carefully instrumented, and if the depressurisation wave outpaces the crack propagation, the forces pulling the pipe apart will reduce at the crack site, and the crack will stop propagating (eventually).

If the crack propagates faster than the depressurisation wave - the entire pipeline is at risk of just - exploding.

Content: This is awesome, when I was an electrician apprentice I got to work on a compressor station. I remember hearing about the pig launcher too but never actually got to see it. Author: @carltonhealy9457
Content:
Let's say we're dealing with a vertical well that generates dry natural gas, no crude oil or water. 
Let's say reservoir rock is 30 ft thick.
Let's say this one vertical well drains a quarter section (basically one quarter mile by one quarter mile) 
Let's also say that porosity is 30%, meaning the rock is 70% grains/minerals and 30% open pore space filled with natural gas. 
Let's also say the recovery factor is only 40%, meaning after all the years of producing the well we drain it as far as current technology allows, and 60% of the natural gas remains trapped in the rock. 

That all comes out to 6.3 million cubic feet of natural gas coming out of that single well. 

BUT that's all calculated at reservoir temperature and pressures.
At standard temperature and pressure the "Standard Cubic Feet" volume of all that natural gas would be much much more.

Author: @krazykrispy21
Content: As a geologist, I'd like to point out that oil and gas don't come from caverns underground, they virtually always come from the natural porosity in between the grains that make up the rock. Just like you can encounter groundwater in the soil by digging down to the water table, you can encounter gas and oil in the actual rock by digging to a formation holding the hydrocarbons in it's pore spaces. This same pore space can be used to store gas or carbon dioxide after it is injected, as well. Some salt caverns are used for this process, but those are relatively uncommon.
